title: Probability & expectation
question: How do we turn uncertain outcomes into a useful average?
intuition: A distribution allocates one unit of belief across possible outcomes. Expectation weights each value by how often it occurs.
steps: List possible outcomes.
Assign nonnegative probabilities that sum to one.
Multiply each value by its probability, then add.
example: A fair die has expected value 3.5, even though you will never roll 3.5.
caveat: An expectation need not be a possible outcome. The distribution still matters: equal means can hide very different risks.
origin: Probability theory grew from questions about uncertain games. Here it supplies the averaging operation that turns surprise into entropy.
check: An event pays 10 with probability 0.2 and 0 otherwise. What is its expected payoff?

title: Surprise / self-information
question: How much did learning one outcome tell you?
intuition: A rare outcome should tell you more. Independent discoveries should add their information, even though their probabilities multiply.
steps: Require information to decrease as probability increases.
Require I(pq) = I(p) + I(q) for independent events.
A negative logarithm does both; base 2 measures bits.
example: A fair coin outcome gives 1 bit. A particular result among 8 equally likely outcomes gives 3 bits.
caveat: Surprise measures an outcome under a model, not emotional surprise. A zero-probability event has infinite surprise if it occurs.
origin: Shannon’s 1948 communication theory connects probability to the length of efficient messages. The logarithm makes independent information additive.
check: Why does an outcome with probability 1/4 carry 2 bits?
answer: Two independent fair binary decisions have probability 1/4; their 1-bit contributions add.

title: Entropy
question: Before observing anything, how much surprise should you expect?
intuition: Average the surprise of every possible outcome, using the true probabilities as weights.
steps: Each outcome costs −log₂ p(x) bits ideally.
It occurs a fraction p(x) of the time.
Add the weighted costs to get average uncertainty.
example: A fair coin averages 1 bit. A 90/10 coin averages about 0.469 bits: its rare outcome is surprising, but rare.
caveat: This is discrete Shannon entropy. Differential entropy for continuous variables behaves differently and can be negative. Use 0 log 0 = 0.
origin: Shannon (1948) asked how efficiently messages can be encoded. Entropy characterizes the asymptotic average lossless coding limit.
check: Can a rare event have high surprise while the whole distribution has low entropy?
answer: Yes. Entropy weights that large surprise by the event’s small probability.

title: Cross-entropy
question: What if your code is designed for the wrong probabilities?
intuition: Keep drawing outcomes from reality P, but assign code lengths using your prediction Q.
steps: Reality still supplies the weights p(x).
Your model supplies the surprise −log₂ q(x).
Average model surprise under reality.
example: If reality is 50/50 but Q predicts 90/10, the average cost is about 1.737 bits instead of 1.
caveat: The first argument supplies the averaging distribution. Changing Q does not change H(P). Natural logs give nats rather than bits.
origin: The coding view extends naturally to prediction: log loss charges a model for how surprised it is by what actually happens.
check: Why is confident misclassification expensive?
answer: It assigns tiny q to the observed class, making −log q very large.

title: KL divergence
question: How much extra cost comes only from using the wrong model?
intuition: Subtract the uncertainty you cannot avoid from the cost of coding with Q. What remains is the mismatch penalty.
steps: Cross-entropy is the total cost under Q.
Entropy is the ideal cost under P.
Subtract: the logarithms combine into a probability ratio.
formula: Dₖₗ(P ‖ Q) = H(P,Q) − H(P) = Σₓ p(x) log₂[p(x)/q(x)]
example: For P = (0.5,0.5), Q = (0.9,0.1): KL ≈ 0.737 bits. Reverse the arguments and it is ≈ 0.531 bits.
caveat: KL is nonnegative but is not a distance metric: it is asymmetric. If p(x)>0 and q(x)=0, it is infinite.
origin: Kullback and Leibler’s 1951 paper studied information for distinguishing statistical populations. The extra-code-length view gives a useful interpretation.
check: If Q becomes exactly P, does cross-entropy become zero?
answer: No: KL becomes zero, while cross-entropy becomes H(P).

title: Joint & conditional entropy
question: How much uncertainty remains when you learn part of the story?
intuition: Joint entropy describes a pair together. Conditional entropy averages the uncertainty about X after Y is known.
steps: Encode Y first.
Then encode X with the distribution appropriate to that Y.
The two average costs add to the joint cost.
example: If Y is an exact copy of a fair bit X, H(X,Y)=1 bit and H(X|Y)=0. Independent fair bits need 2 bits together.
caveat: Conditional entropy averages over Y; it is not the entropy for just one chosen value y. “Multiple-entropy” is not a standard single term; joint entropy handles several variables.
origin: Chain rules in information theory account for messages in parts and expose what can be saved by exploiting dependence.
check: Why do two copies of the same bit not carry two bits of information?
answer: Once you know the first, the second adds no uncertainty or new information.

title: Mutual information
question: How much does knowing one variable tell you about another?
intuition: Measure the uncertainty removed from X by observing Y. Equivalently, compare the real joint distribution with an independent one.
steps: Start with uncertainty H(X).
Subtract the remaining uncertainty H(X|Y).
The saving is shared information, symmetric in X and Y.
example: A fair bit and its copy share 1 bit. Independent fair bits share 0.
caveat: Dependence does not imply causation. Continuous deterministic neural representations can make mutual-information estimation subtle or divergent.
origin: Mutual information formalizes how a received signal reduces uncertainty about a transmitted one; it becomes a tool for studying representations.
check: Can independent variables each have high entropy but zero mutual information?
answer: Yes. Each may be unpredictable without revealing anything about the other.

title: Markov chains
question: How much history must a process remember?
intuition: The present state can be a sufficient summary of the past for predicting the next state.
steps: Choose a state description.
Give transition probabilities from each current state.
Repeatedly sample the next state using only the current one.
example: A weather toy has sunny → sunny probability 0.8 and rainy → sunny probability 0.3. Tomorrow’s distribution follows from today’s state.
caveat: Markov does not mean independent across time. Whether the assumption holds depends on what you include in the state.
origin: Markov studied dependent sequences rather than only independent trials. Modern diffusion models use chains to add and remove noise.
check: If tomorrow depends on today, can the process still be Markov?
answer: Yes. It is dependence on earlier history beyond the current state that the Markov property excludes.

title: Data processing inequality
question: Can processing recover information that has already disappeared?
intuition: In a Markov chain X → T → Z, Z only sees X through T. It cannot learn distinctions that T erased.
steps: T supplies everything Z can observe about X.
Any distinctions lost before T are unavailable downstream.
Therefore information about X cannot increase.
example: If a photo is reduced to “contains an animal,” later processing cannot recover the animal’s original pixel colors from that bit alone.
caveat: The Markov condition matters: a later stage receiving extra side information can gain information. Better prediction can still follow easier-to-use representations.
origin: A central information-theory constraint explains why useful representation learning is about preserving and reorganizing information, not creating it about the original sample.
check: Can a later layer classify better even though it cannot increase input information?
answer: Yes. It can make the relevant information easier for a simple decision rule to use.

title: Representation learning
question: Why should a model learn features instead of receiving them by hand?
intuition: Change coordinates so that useful distinctions become easier to express. Hidden layers are learned descriptions of the input.
steps: Raw inputs contain many entangled factors.
Transform them through learned layers.
Optimize the transformations for a task or learning signal.
example: Pixels become edge-like patterns, then shapes or task-relevant features. This is an intuition, not a required hierarchy in every network.
caveat: A representation can also encode shortcuts and nuisance variables. Good training accuracy does not prove useful features.
origin: Learning features reduces dependence on manually engineered descriptions. The ATDL information-bottleneck notes ask which information these features retain.
check: Is a hidden representation necessarily a compressed vector?
answer: No. It can have more coordinates than the input; compression can refer to information or description length instead.

title: Information bottleneck
question: What should a representation forget?
intuition: Keep what predicts Y while discarding other details of X. Compression has a purpose only relative to what you want to preserve.
steps: Measure retained input information I(X;T).
Measure predictive information I(T;Y).
Penalize the first and reward the second.
example: For classifying handwritten digits, pen color may be expendable while stroke shape is useful.
caveat: The mathematical objective is distinct from the claim that ordinary SGD automatically solves it. Information estimates in deterministic networks require care.
origin: Tishby, Pereira and Bialek (1999) formulated a compression–prediction trade-off using ideas from rate–distortion theory.
check: What happens when β is increased?
answer: Preserving predictive information receives more weight relative to compression.

title: Information plane
question: How can we watch the information content of layers change?
intuition: Place each layer at coordinates describing input information retained and target information retained.
steps: Estimate I(X;T) for the horizontal axis.
Estimate I(T;Y) for the vertical axis.
Follow a layer’s estimated position during training.
example: Moving up means more target information; moving left means less input information. Up and left is the desired IB direction when feasible.
caveat: Trajectories depend on estimators, binning and architecture. The two-phase compression story is a research claim, not a universal law.
origin: Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby (2017) used information-plane plots to interpret training. Saxe and colleagues later challenged the generality of the compression explanation.
check: Does moving left alone prove learning improved?
answer: No. It could mean throwing away predictive information too; check the vertical axis and held-out performance.

title: Lagrange multipliers
question: How can a constraint become part of an objective?
intuition: Assign a price to violating a constraint. The multiplier expresses how much objective value you exchange for relaxing it.
steps: Write an objective and constraint.
Add a multiplier times the constraint residual.
Solve the resulting stationarity and feasibility conditions.
example: In IB, β acts as the relative price of losing predictive information: I(X;T) − βI(T;Y).
caveat: A weighted objective and a constrained problem are not always interchangeable globally, especially in nonconvex settings.
origin: Lagrange’s constrained-optimization method provides the mathematical language for many modern fit-versus-complexity trade-offs.
check: What does a large multiplier tell you intuitively?
answer: The associated constraint or reward strongly influences the optimum; violating it is expensive.

title: Empirical risk minimization
question: How do we optimize performance when the true data distribution is unknown?
intuition: Replace an inaccessible population average with an average over observed training examples.
steps: Choose a loss that measures prediction error.
Average it on the sample.
Find parameters with low sample loss.
example: Minimizing average classification cross-entropy over your dataset is ERM.
caveat: Low empirical risk is not necessarily low population risk. Reusing the test set for model selection defeats its purpose.
origin: Statistical learning theory asks when fitting a finite sample also yields reliable predictions on new draws.
check: Why is training loss called empirical?
answer: It is measured on the observed sample instead of averaged over the unknown population.

title: Gradients & backpropagation
question: Which small parameter changes will reduce the loss?
intuition: A gradient reports local sensitivity to each parameter. Backpropagation computes these sensitivities efficiently by reusing the chain rule.
steps: Run the network forward to compute loss.
Send sensitivities backward through each operation.
Combine them to obtain each parameter derivative.
example: If h=wx and L=h², then ∂L/∂w = 2hx. With w=2, x=3, the derivative is 36.
caveat: Backpropagation computes a gradient; an optimizer decides how to use it. Local downhill motion does not guarantee a global minimum.
origin: Reverse-mode differentiation made learning many parameters practical by sharing derivative computations through a graph.
check: Are backpropagation and gradient descent the same thing?
answer: No. One computes derivatives; the other updates parameters using them.

title: Stochastic gradient descent
question: Can we learn without inspecting every example before each update?
intuition: A random mini-batch gives a cheaper, noisy estimate of the full training gradient.
steps: Sample a mini-batch.
Average its loss gradients.
Step opposite the estimated gradient and repeat.
example: With gradient 2, parameter 3, and learning rate 0.1, the next parameter is 2.8.
caveat: An unbiased gradient estimate requires appropriate sampling. Large steps can diverge, and noise alone does not guarantee generalization.
origin: Stochastic approximation, including Robbins–Monro (1951), provided methods for finding solutions from noisy observations.
check: Why can two mini-batches suggest different directions?
answer: They contain different examples, so their gradient estimates fluctuate around the full-data gradient.

title: Batches, steps & epochs
question: How much training has actually happened?
intuition: A step updates parameters once. A batch supplies that update. An epoch is approximately one pass over the dataset.
steps: Divide the dataset into batches.
Perform one update per batch.
Completing the pass counts as one epoch.
example: 10,000 examples at batch size 1,000 give 10 updates per epoch.
caveat: Dropping the last batch uses floor instead of ceiling. Streaming or replacement sampling needs an explicitly defined epoch convention.
origin: These bookkeeping units emerged from iterative dataset training. They are essential when comparing compute and learning curves.
check: If batch size doubles, do steps per epoch double?
answer: They approximately halve, for a fixed dataset size.

title: Signal-to-noise ratio
question: Is a gradient mostly consistent direction or random fluctuation?
intuition: Compare the magnitude of the mean gradient with variation across stochastic gradient estimates.
steps: Collect gradients from batches.
Estimate their mean and variation.
Compare consistent motion with random spread.
example: A mean gradient of magnitude 2 with RMS noise 0.5 has SNR 4 under this convention.
caveat: SNR conventions differ, including squared ratios. Near a stationary point the mean may shrink even if noise also decreases.
origin: Signal-versus-noise language comes from measurement and communication and helps describe stochastic training dynamics.
check: Can SNR fall without noise becoming larger?
answer: Yes. The mean gradient may shrink while the noise stays similar.

title: Stochastic relaxation
question: What can weights do after average downhill motion becomes weak?
intuition: Batch-to-batch fluctuations can keep parameters moving among similarly low-loss configurations.
steps: Early gradients may point consistently downhill.
Later the mean can become small relative to noise.
Model the resulting motion approximately as diffusion.
example: Think of a walker in a shallow valley: weak drift along the floor, with random sideways kicks.
caveat: The proposed link from this motion to information compression is paper-specific and disputed. SGD noise is generally neither constant nor isotropic.
origin: The ATDL 2017 information-bottleneck paper interprets a later phase as diffusion-driven compression; subsequent work limits that interpretation.
check: Does noisy late training necessarily compress every neural network?
answer: No. This is a hypothesis whose behavior depends on the model, data and information estimator.

title: L1 & L2 regularization
question: How do we discourage fitting every accidental detail?
intuition: Add a cost for parameter choices you want the model to avoid. L1 favors sparsity; L2 shrinks weights smoothly.
steps: Start with empirical loss.
Add a penalty scaled by λ.
Optimize the combined objective.
formula: L1: R̂ + λΣ|wⱼ|;   L2: R̂ + λΣwⱼ²
example: For weights (3,4), L1=7 and squared L2=25, before multiplying by λ.
caveat: Exact L1 zeros depend on optimization; naive gradient updates may not produce them. Weight decay and L2 penalties differ for some adaptive optimizers.
origin: Penalty methods encode preferences for simpler or more stable solutions; they connect to Bayesian priors and description length.
check: Which penalty keeps exerting a constant-magnitude pull toward zero away from zero?
answer: L1. L2’s derivative scales with the weight magnitude.

title: Multilayer perceptrons
question: How do simple units compose a nonlinear predictor?
intuition: Alternate linear mixing with nonlinear activations. Hidden layers let the model learn intermediate features.
steps: Mix inputs with weights and biases.
Apply an activation separately to units.
Repeat, then produce a prediction.
example: A two-layer network can combine simple threshold-like responses into a more complex decision boundary.
caveat: Stacking only affine layers is still one affine transformation. Nonlinear activations are essential for nonlinear expressiveness.
origin: Perceptron-style units became more expressive when composed in layers and trained through derivatives.
check: What happens if every activation is replaced by the identity?
answer: The entire network collapses to one affine transformation, regardless of depth.

title: Binarized neural networks
question: Can a network work with just two weight values?
intuition: Use weights such as −1 and +1 to reduce representation and arithmetic costs and expose discrete structural patterns.
steps: Maintain or optimize trainable parameters.
Binarize values used in the forward pass.
Use a gradient approximation to update trainable parameters.
example: A 4×4 binary weight matrix can be displayed as a black-and-white tile and analyzed for repeated patterns.
caveat: Here BNN means binarized, not Bayesian neural network. Actual speed and storage gains depend on kernels and training implementation.
origin: The ATDL BNN paper uses discrete weight matrices to study whether training increases algorithmic structure.
check: Why are binary weights convenient for block decomposition?
answer: They directly form discrete patterns that can be split into small blocks with estimated description lengths.

title: Straight-through estimator
question: How can learning pass through a discrete operation?
intuition: Use the discrete operation forward, but substitute a useful derivative backward.
steps: Compute sign(w) for the forward prediction.
Its true derivative is zero almost everywhere.
Replace that derivative with a surrogate during backpropagation.
example: A weight at 0.3 outputs +1, while a clipped-identity surrogate still lets its underlying real parameter receive a gradient.
caveat: This is a biased gradient heuristic, not the exact derivative of the discrete objective. Surrogates differ.
origin: Bengio and colleagues (2013) discussed estimating gradients through stochastic and discrete neurons.
check: Is the STE the true derivative of sign?
answer: No. It deliberately substitutes another derivative so optimization can proceed.

title: Kolmogorov–Chaitin complexity
question: How long is the shortest recipe for an object?
intuition: A pattern is simple if a short program can generate it, even when its symbol frequencies look random.
steps: Fix a universal description language.
Consider programs that output the object and halt.
Take the length of the shortest one.
example: “Repeat 01 fifty times” describes a 100-bit alternating string compactly, although its zero/one entropy is maximal.
caveat: Exact Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable in general and depends on the reference machine up to an additive constant.
origin: Solomonoff, Kolmogorov and Chaitin developed algorithmic accounts of randomness and description length in the 1960s.
check: Why can Shannon symbol entropy miss structure?
answer: It can see balanced symbol counts while ignoring a simple rule that determines their ordering.

title: Algorithmic probability
question: Which outputs are likely when the input is a random program?
intuition: Outputs with short descriptions receive substantial probability mass because short programs are easier to sample.
steps: Use a prefix-free universal machine.
Weight each halting program by 2 to minus its length.
Sum weights of programs that output the same object.
example: A 5-bit program contributes 1/32 probability mass; a 20-bit program contributes about one millionth.
caveat: This is a semimeasure because some programs never halt. The coding theorem has an additive constant, not exact equality.
origin: Algorithmic probability links induction to program length; the coding theorem connects probability with algorithmic complexity.
check: Why specify prefix-free programs?
answer: They permit a valid probability weighting by length without ambiguously counting a program and its extensions.

title: Coding theorem method
question: Can small program experiments approximate algorithmic complexity?
intuition: Run a finite family of small machines and use output frequencies as an empirical proxy for algorithmic probability.
steps: Enumerate a chosen finite machine space.
Run with a stated halting or time-limit convention and tally outputs.
Transform frequencies using −log₂.
example: An output appearing with frequency 1/8 gets a proxy value of 3 bits under that empirical distribution.
caveat: Finite enumeration and runtime cutoffs are approximations. In the ATDL convention the machine count grows as (4n+2)^(2n), not 2 raised to output length.
origin: CTM brings the coding-theorem idea to small computable tables, at the cost of severe enumeration limits.
check: Does CTM enumerate every program that could produce a chosen x?
answer: No. It runs a finite chosen machine family first and then counts the outputs it observes.

title: Block decomposition method
question: How can small complexity tables say anything about a large matrix?
intuition: Split a large object into small blocks, pay once for each distinct block, and add a cost for repetition counts.
steps: Decompose into blocks supported by a CTM table.
Group identical blocks.
Sum estimated block complexity plus log₂ multiplicity.
formula: BDM(X) ≈ Σ distinct r [CTM(r) + log₂ nᵣ]
example: If the same block appears 8 times, its contribution is CTM(block)+3 rather than eight full CTM costs.
caveat: Block size, boundary handling and lost long-range arrangement affect the estimate. BDM is not exact Kolmogorov complexity.
origin: BDM extends small-output CTM estimates to larger discrete objects; the ATDL paper applies it to binary network weights.
check: What structure might BDM miss with very small blocks?
answer: Dependencies and arrangement spanning several blocks can be lost.

title: Minimum description length
question: When does a more elaborate model earn its extra complexity?
intuition: Pay for both the model and what the model leaves unexplained. A useful model saves more data-description bits than it costs.
steps: Encode the model.
Encode the observations using that model.
Minimize their combined length.
example: Model A costs 10+100=110 bits; model B costs 30+60=90 bits. B wins despite being larger.
caveat: MDL is a model-selection principle with specified codes, not the uncomputable shortest program definition of K(x).
origin: Rissanen’s 1978 formulation connected statistical modeling to data compression.
check: Does MDL always choose the smallest model?
answer: No. A larger model can win by saving more bits when encoding the data.

title: Pearson correlation
question: Do two quantities move together approximately linearly?
intuition: Center both variables and measure how aligned their deviations are, normalized by their spread.
steps: Subtract the mean from each variable.
Average products of deviations.
Divide by the product of standard deviations.
example: [1,2,3,4] and [9,10,11,12] have r=1. A vertical shift does not alter linear alignment.
caveat: Correlation is not causation, is sensitive to outliers, and is undefined if either variable is constant.
origin: The ATDL complexity paper uses linear association to compare loss trajectories with complexity estimates.
check: Does a higher correlation with loss prove better model accuracy?
answer: No. It measures how closely two quantities vary together, not which trained model performs best.

title: Spearman rank correlation
question: Do two quantities preserve ordering, even on a curve?
intuition: Replace values by ranks, then compute Pearson correlation on those ranks.
steps: Rank each variable, averaging tied ranks.
Compare the paired ranks.
Strong monotonic agreement gives a value near 1.
example: [1,2,3,4] and [1,4,9,16] have ρ=1 even though the relation is quadratic.
caveat: It detects monotonic association, not arbitrary dependence. Non-monotonic relationships can have low rank correlation.
origin: Rank methods compare ordering without requiring a linear relation or identical scales.
check: Can Spearman be 1 while Pearson is less than 1?
answer: Yes: a strictly increasing nonlinear relationship preserves ranks without lying on a straight line.

title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
question: How uncertain is an estimate when only a finite sample is available?
intuition: Resample the observed independent units with replacement and see how much the statistic changes.
steps: Draw a bootstrap sample of the same size with replacement.
Recompute the statistic; repeat many times.
Construct an interval using a stated bootstrap method.
example: For a study with 30 independent training runs, resample runs—not individual time steps as though they were independent.
caveat: A frequentist 95% procedure targets 95% coverage across repeated studies; it does not assign 95% probability to the fixed parameter in this one realized interval.
origin: Efron’s bootstrap (1979) made resampling a practical route to sampling uncertainty. The ATDL paper uses resampled runs for correlation intervals.
check: Why not independently resample every time step from one training curve?
answer: Time steps are dependent; treating them as independent exaggerates the amount of information.

title: Generalization & bias–variance
question: Why can a perfect fit still predict badly?
intuition: Training sees one finite sample. A model can fit sample-specific accidents instead of stable relationships.
steps: Separate training and held-out observations.
Compare fit with out-of-sample error.
For squared error, separate systematic bias, sample variability and irreducible noise.
formula: E[(Y−f̂(X))²] = noise + bias² + variance (under the usual regression assumptions)
example: A very flexible curve may hit every training point but swing wildly between them.
caveat: Bias–variance is a decomposition, not a theorem that variance must increase monotonically with parameter count.
origin: Classical learning theory formalized the difference between fitting observations and predicting fresh samples; ATDL examines how deep networks complicate simple capacity stories.
check: What does a widening training–test gap suggest?
answer: The model is improving on its observed sample without equivalent improvement on new data.

title: Bayesian inference & evidence
question: How should observations update uncertainty about a model?
intuition: Multiply prior plausibility by the likelihood of the observations, then normalize. Evidence averages fit across the prior’s possibilities.
steps: Choose a prior p(θ).
Evaluate likelihood p(D|θ).
Normalize their product by p(D) to obtain the posterior.
example: A model with one tiny region of excellent fit need not have high evidence if most of its prior mass predicts poorly.
caveat: MAP selects one posterior mode; evidence integrates over parameters. SGD is not generally an exact posterior sampler.
origin: Bayesian inference turns learning into probability updating. ATDL connects evidence and local loss geometry with optimization.
check: Is evidence simply the maximum likelihood achieved by a model?
answer: No. It averages likelihood under the prior rather than taking its maximum.

title: PAC–Bayes bounds
question: Can we bound unseen error even with many more weights than examples?
intuition: Bound the expected risk of a distribution Q over predictors using training risk and its divergence from a data-independent prior P.
steps: Fix a valid prior before observing the training sample.
Learn a distribution Q with low empirical risk.
Pay a confidence and KL-dependent complexity term.
formula: schematic: true risk ≲ empirical risk + √[(KL(Q‖P)+confidence term)/n]
example: A bound of 0.2 on an error rate is informative; a bound above 1 is vacuous because an error rate is already at most 1.
caveat: The display is schematic, not a plug-in theorem. Exact bounds require specified loss range, sampling assumptions, constants and confidence level.
origin: Dziugaite and Roy (2017) computed nonvacuous PAC–Bayes bounds for overparameterized stochastic neural networks.
check: Why can’t a standard prior be freely fitted to the same sample?
answer: The theorem’s independence requirement would fail; data-dependent priors need a valid adjusted construction.

title: Double descent
question: Why can test error improve again after a model can fit everything?
intuition: Test error can rise near the interpolation threshold and then fall as capacity grows further.
steps: At low capacity the model underfits.
Near interpolation, fitting all points can be unstable.
Farther beyond it, the selected solution can generalize better again.
formula: interpolation threshold: training error first reaches ≈ 0
example: A model-size sweep can produce a decline, a peak near interpolation, and a second decline in test error.
caveat: It is a phenomenon seen in particular settings, not a promise that making any model bigger improves it. Regularization and noise can change the curve.
origin: Nakkiran and colleagues extended double-descent observations to deep networks and effective capacity, including training duration.
check: Why doesn’t double descent contradict the bias–variance identity?
answer: The identity does not require either component to vary monotonically with parameter count.

title: Grokking
question: Can generalization arrive long after memorization?
intuition: In some tasks, training accuracy saturates early while test accuracy improves only after much more optimization.
steps: First fit the observed examples.
Continue optimization with the chosen training setup.
A more general rule may eventually become dominant.
formula: time to fit training data ≪ time to generalize (in a grokking regime)
example: On modular arithmetic, a network may memorize observed pairs before acquiring a rule that works on unseen pairs.
caveat: Grokking is task- and setup-dependent. Continued training does not guarantee it; monitor held-out data without selecting on the final test set.
origin: The ATDL Liu et al. paper studies an effective theory of representation learning to explain delayed generalization.
check: What distinguishes grokking from ordinary fast learning?
answer: A substantial delay separates near-perfect training performance from improved unseen-data performance.

title: Mosaic-of-Motifs
question: Can we encourage weight matrices to reuse a small vocabulary of patterns?
intuition: Represent a matrix as small motifs plus a map saying which motif each block uses.
steps: Split the weights into blocks.
Choose a small motif bank.
Assign blocks to motifs and reconstruct structured weights.
example: A matrix with 100 blocks chosen from 4 motifs can reuse those motifs instead of storing 100 unrelated blocks.
caveat: Motif number and block size restrict capacity. Reduced description length does not by itself guarantee accuracy or measured hardware speed.
origin: The ATDL MoMos lecture motivates algorithmic simplification as a structured parameterization, with projection toward motif reuse.
check: What changes when the motif bank becomes larger?
answer: Capacity and storage cost can increase because blocks have more distinct patterns available.

title: Likelihood & generative modeling
question: Can a model learn what data looks like, rather than only its label?
intuition: A generative model describes a distribution over observations, often through hidden variables or a sampling procedure.
steps: Choose a family of distributions or samplers.
Fit it using observations.
Draw new samples or evaluate predictions under the learned model.
formula: maxθ Σᵢ log pθ(xᵢ)  ⇔  minθ average negative log-likelihood
example: A model of handwritten digits learns a distribution over digit images, allowing it to generate new ones.
caveat: Not every generative model exposes a tractable likelihood. High likelihood and perceptual quality need not rank models identically.
origin: Generative modeling extends density estimation to rich structured data. ATDL topic 2 compares several ways to represent and train these distributions.
check: What is the relation between likelihood training and cross-entropy?
answer: Average negative log-likelihood is empirical cross-entropy under the model distribution.

title: Latent variables
question: How can hidden causes make complicated observations easier to model?
intuition: Introduce unobserved variables that describe factors behind the data, then generate observations conditional on them.
steps: Sample a hidden variable z from a prior.
Generate x using pθ(x|z).
Integrate out z to describe the observed-data distribution.
example: A low-dimensional z might control digit shape and stroke thickness before a decoder produces pixels.
caveat: Learned latent coordinates are not automatically interpretable or disentangled; multiple latent descriptions can explain the same data.
origin: Latent-variable models separate hidden structure from observed variation. Neural decoders make that structure highly flexible.
check: Is a latent variable necessarily a class label?
answer: No. It can be continuous, discrete, multidimensional, or unrelated to human labels.

title: Variational autoencoders & ELBO
question: How do we train a latent model when the true posterior is intractable?
intuition: Learn an approximate posterior and maximize a tractable lower bound on log-likelihood.
steps: Use qφ(z|x) to infer likely latent causes.
Reward reconstruction under the decoder.
Penalize divergence from the latent prior.
formula: ELBO = E_q[log pθ(x|z)] − KL(qφ(z|x) ‖ p(z)) ≤ log pθ(x)
example: An encoder produces Gaussian mean and scale; z=μ+σε lets reconstruction gradients reach those parameters.
caveat: The KL term here compares a per-example latent posterior with its prior, not the data distribution directly. Too strong a penalty can cause posterior collapse.
origin: Kingma and Welling’s Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (2013) made neural variational inference practical with reparameterized gradients.
check: Why is the ELBO only a lower bound?
answer: Its gap to log pθ(x) is KL(qφ(z|x) ‖ pθ(z|x)), which is nonnegative.

title: Generative adversarial networks
question: Can a model learn to generate without evaluating its own density?
intuition: A generator makes examples while a discriminator learns to distinguish generated examples from real ones.
steps: Generate samples from noise.
Train a discriminator using real and generated data.
Train the generator to improve against that discriminator.
example: A discriminator notices missing stroke patterns; its feedback changes the generator toward more plausible digits.
caveat: This is the original minimax objective; practical losses differ. Training can be unstable and can omit modes of the data distribution.
origin: Goodfellow and colleagues (2014) introduced adversarial training as a way to learn a generative model through a learned critic.
check: What is mode collapse?
answer: The generator produces too little diversity, repeatedly covering only some kinds of real examples.

title: Normalizing flows
question: Can a complex density come from a reversible transformation?
intuition: Transform a simple distribution through invertible maps while tracking how volumes change.
steps: Sample z from a simple base distribution.
Apply invertible x=f(z).
Correct density by the transformation’s Jacobian determinant.
formula: log p_X(x) = log p_Z(f⁻¹(x)) + log |det J_f⁻¹(x)|
example: Stretching a one-dimensional interval to twice its length halves its density.
caveat: Invertibility and tractable Jacobians constrain architectures. Continuous flows replace finite maps with differential equations.
origin: The change-of-variables rule provides the basis for flow-based density models; learned transforms give flexible distributions.
check: Why does a density need a volume correction?
answer: Probability mass stays the same when coordinates stretch, so density per unit volume must change.

title: Diffusion / DDPM
question: Can generating a complex image be broken into simple denoising decisions?
intuition: Gradually corrupt data with known noise, then learn how to reverse the corruption.
steps: Choose a forward Gaussian noising schedule.
Train a network to predict injected noise or an equivalent target.
Start from noise and apply learned reverse steps.
example: Early noisy digits retain shape; at high noise the input nearly loses its identity. A denoiser learns across these noise levels.
caveat: Reverse generation is not simply subtracting the exact sampled training noise. Standard sampling uses a learned conditional reverse process.
origin: DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) made high-quality generation practical with a simple noise-prediction objective, building on earlier diffusion modeling.
check: Why can we form a noisy training example without simulating every previous step?
answer: The Gaussian forward chain has a closed-form marginal at each chosen time t.

title: Score matching
question: Which direction leads toward more probable data?
intuition: The score is the gradient of log density with respect to the sample, not the model weights.
steps: Take log p(x).
Differentiate with respect to x.
Learn this vector field, often using noisy data and denoising targets.
example: For a standard Gaussian, s(x)=−x: the score points toward the high-density center.
caveat: Following the score deterministically to a mode is not the same as sampling the distribution. Sampling requires an appropriate dynamics or probability-flow construction.
origin: Score matching avoids needing the normalizing constant of a density; noise-conditioned scores connect it to modern diffusion samplers.
check: What variable is differentiated in the score?
answer: The data coordinate x. A training gradient usually differentiates loss with respect to parameters θ.

title: ODEs & numerical sampling
question: How can local velocity define an entire trajectory?
intuition: An ordinary differential equation gives the direction and speed of motion at every state and time.
steps: Specify an initial state.
Evaluate the velocity field.
Integrate it over time, approximating with finite steps in a computer.
formula: dx/dt = v(x,t);  Euler: xₜ₊Δₜ ≈ xₜ + Δt v(xₜ,t)
example: For dx/dt=−x, a step of 0.1 moves x=1 to 0.9 by Euler; the exact value is exp(−0.1)≈0.9048.
caveat: Large steps can introduce error or instability. Existence and uniqueness need conditions on the field.
origin: Differential equations describe motion through local rules. Generative flows use the same machinery to transport random samples.
check: Why can fewer sampling steps reduce quality?
answer: A coarse numerical approximation may poorly track the learned trajectory.

title: Flow matching & rectified flow
question: How can a network learn to move noise into data without solving an ODE during training?
intuition: Give the network many noisy intermediate states and teach it the local direction of motion. At generation time, follow the learned directions backward in small steps.
steps: Choose a data example x and independent Gaussian noise ε. In this chapter, data is at time 0 and noise at time 1.
Choose t and mix them: zₜ=(1−t)x+tε. Differentiating this straight conditional path gives the available target ε−x.
Feed zₜ and t to a velocity network. Minimize squared error against ε−x; compatible pairs collectively teach a marginal velocity field.
Start from new noise at t=1. Repeatedly predict the velocity and take a backward solver step until t=0.
formula: LFM = E[‖vθ(zₜ,t) − (ε−x)‖²];    zₜ₋ₕ ≈ zₜ − h vθ(zₜ,t)
example: Take x=−1, ε=2 and t=0.6. The mixed state is −0.4+1.2=0.8, and the training velocity is 3. A prediction of 0.62 has squared error (0.62−3)²=5.6644. The minus sign in generation reverses the data-to-noise velocity.
caveat: A straight path for one paired example does not imply straight trajectories of the learned marginal field. This is the independent-pair linear-path case, not every path allowed by Flow Matching, and not an implementation of optimal transport pairing or reflow.
origin: Flow matching and rectified flow developed closely related velocity-learning approaches. Lipman et al. (2022) frame flow matching through probability paths.
check: Is the learned velocity necessarily the displacement of one specific paired example?
answer: No. Regression averages compatible conditional targets at a state and time.

study.subtitle: Learn a local direction. Repeat it to travel.
study.change: Start with the shared path, a time-conditioned network, and ordinary velocity regression.

sections.title: Read the symbols before the equations
body: x is a real example; ε (epsilon) is random noise; zₜ is an intermediate state. A state can be one number, a point with two coordinates, or thousands of image-latent coordinates. Bold vectors are not necessary here: the same arithmetic acts on every coordinate.

Throughout these three sections, t=0 means data and t=1 means noise. Generation travels backward, from 1 to 0. This reverses the convention used in some flow-matching presentations but does not change the underlying method. r is an earlier, less noisy time; 0 ≤ r ≤ t ≤ 1. h=t−r is the jump length.

θ (theta) names all learnable network weights. v means instantaneous velocity: motion per unit time right now. u means average velocity over a specified interval. E means an average over random training examples. ‖error‖² means square each coordinate error and add them. sg means keep a computed value but stop gradients through that branch.
sections.formula: zₜ = (1−t)x + tε     h = t−r     v꜀ = ε−x

sections.title: 1. A distribution is a cloud, not one destination
body: Imagine each noise sample as a dot in a cloud. We want the whole cloud to end up shaped like the data cloud. No label tells a fresh random dot which particular photograph it must become. A learned vector field supplies a direction at every visited state and time.

For training, we can invent easy paths between sampled endpoints. With the straight interpolation above, the derivative is −x+ε because the endpoints stay fixed while t changes. We therefore get a target without running the learned model to create a trajectory. This is why the training objective is called simulation-free: training-state construction needs no ODE solver.
sections.formula: d[(1−t)x+tε]/dt = ε−x

sections.title: 2. Why matching pairs learns a field
body: Different endpoint pairs can pass through the same state. Their velocity labels may disagree. A deterministic network only sees the state and time, so squared-error fitting encourages the average compatible velocity, called the marginal velocity.
For example, two equally likely labels 1 and 3 at the same input are best predicted by 2. The loss is ((q−1)²+(q−3)²)/2=(q−2)²+1. The unavoidable 1 is label variation, not a model failure.

More generally, conditional squared error separates into distance from E[v꜀|z,t] plus conditional variance. Under regularity conditions, this marginal field transports the selected probability path: the density satisfies the continuity equation. We are describing a population optimum; finite data, imperfect networks and numerical solvers introduce errors.
sections.formula: v(z,t) = E[ε−x | zₜ=z, t];    ∂ₜpₜ + ∇·(pₜv) = 0

sections.title: 3. Architecture: what passes through the network?
body: Flow Matching specifies a learning objective, not a unique architecture. A small 2D experiment can concatenate the two state coordinates and a time embedding, pass them through an MLP, and output two velocity coordinates. A U-Net or a transformer can instead handle images.

For a fair comparison with the next two papers, the diagram uses a DiT-style latent-image backbone as a teaching example. A fixed VAE encoder compresses an image into a latent grid. Mixing with noise happens in that grid. Patches become token vectors; positional information keeps their spatial arrangement identifiable.

A time embedding, and optionally a class embedding, controls the transformer. In adaLN-style conditioning, learned functions of these embeddings adjust normalization scales, shifts and residual gates. Attention lets each image token gather information from other locations; an MLP transforms each token; residual connections add the update to its incoming representation.

The output projection maps image tokens back to a velocity grid of the same shape as z. A velocity value is a proposed change, not a final pixel color. At sampling time the numerical solver updates the latent, then a VAE decoder turns the final latent into pixels. This illustrative backbone must not be attributed as a mandatory design of the original Flow Matching paper.

In the attention formula, H stacks token vectors in rows; WQ, WK and WV are learned projection matrices. Q, K and V mean queries, keys and values. Kᵀ is the transposed key matrix, d is the key width, and softmax acts across key positions for each query. An output row is therefore a weighted mixture of value vectors, with weights summing to one.
sections.formula: Q=HWQ, K=HWK, V=HWV;    attention(H)=softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V

sections.title: 4. Training and sampling are different algorithms
body: Training: sample a batch of x and ε; sample t; compute z and ε−x; predict velocity; average squared errors; backpropagate into θ; update weights with an optimizer. Repeat across many independent examples. The steps in the microscope below expose a single example inside this process.

Sampling: freeze θ, draw fresh ε, set z=ε and t=1, predict velocity, subtract h times that velocity, reduce t by h, and repeat. Euler uses one prediction per step; Heun typically uses two to better approximate curvature. Count neural function evaluations (NFE), not just outer-loop iterations.

For the analytic toy dz/dt=z with z(1)=2, the exact endpoint is 2/e≈0.73576. One backward Euler step gives 2−2=0. Eight steps give 2(7/8)⁸≈0.68722. More small steps approach the exact solution. This illustrates integration error even when the instantaneous field is known perfectly; it is not a generated-image quality benchmark.
sections.formula: Euler: z ← z − h vθ(z,t);    t ← t−h

sections.title: 5. What problem remains for MeanFlow?
body: A local direction is insufficient to describe a long curved trip with one straight jump. One large Euler step treats the current velocity as constant over the entire interval. Rather than only improving the solver, we can ask a new learning question: can the network predict the average velocity of the whole trip?

Rectified Flow also studies straight interpolations and learned transport, with reflow procedures intended to make learned trajectories straighter. Do not equate all Flow Matching methods with reflow, or interpret an independently sampled pair as an optimal transport coupling. The next chapter changes the predicted quantity itself.
sections.formula: Local information: v(z,t)     →     interval information: u(z,r,t)

architecture: Training x → fixed encoder for images
Same shape as the data representation
Patch tokens + position; embed time t
For 2D, use a small MLP instead
Output has exactly the shape of z
z ← z−h vθ; repeat to t=0
One model call per Euler step
research: Separate field error from integration error: first test solvers on a known analytic field, then test a learned field against a high-accuracy reference integration.

Hypothesis to test, not an established result: a different endpoint coupling may reduce trajectory curvature. Compare identical model size, training budget, solver and evaluation data; measure curvature as well as sample quality.
sources: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling — Lipman et al. (2022), §3–4
Flow Straight and Fast — Liu, Gong & Liu (2022), rectified flow and reflow
Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers — Peebles & Xie (2022), backbone context

title: Conditioning & classifier-free guidance
question: How can a generator follow a prompt more strongly?
intuition: Condition predictions on text or labels, then optionally amplify the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions.
steps: Train with and without conditioning.
Compute both predictions at the same noisy state.
Extrapolate toward the conditional prediction.
example: s=1 gives the conditional prediction under this convention; s>1 amplifies conditioning.
caveat: Large guidance can reduce diversity and create artifacts. Some papers use an offset convention for the scale.
origin: Classifier-free guidance removes the need for a separate noisy-image classifier when steering diffusion models.
check: Under this convention, what does s=0 produce?
answer: The unconditional prediction.

title: Attention & transformers
question: How can each token decide which other tokens matter?
intuition: Compare a query with keys to assign weights, then mix the corresponding values.
steps: Project tokens into queries, keys and values.
Normalize query–key similarities with softmax.
Use the weights to average value vectors.
example: An image patch can attend to nearby edges or a text token naming the object it should depict.
caveat: Attention weights are not automatically causal explanations. Self-attention and cross-attention differ in where queries and keys/values come from.
origin: The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) organized sequence modeling around attention; diffusion transformers apply related blocks to image patches.
check: In cross-attention, must queries and keys come from the same input?
answer: No. Image features may supply queries while text supplies keys and values.

title: Latent diffusion & diffusion transformers
question: Can we denoise a compact representation instead of every pixel?
intuition: An autoencoder compresses images into latents. A denoising model operates there, often with a transformer over latent patches.
steps: Encode an image to a latent representation.
Learn diffusion or flow dynamics in that space.
Decode the generated latent back to pixels.
formula: x → encoder → z;   noise → latent denoiser → ẑ → decoder → x̂
example: A compressed spatial grid reduces the number of locations the generative model must process.
caveat: Compression can lose detail. “Latent diffusion” names the working space; “diffusion transformer” names an architecture, and does not by itself fix the training objective.
origin: Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) reduced generative computation; DiT studied scalable transformer backbones for diffusion.
check: Can a diffusion transformer operate in a latent space?
answer: Yes. The architecture and the representation space are separate design choices.

title: Distillation, consistency & mean velocity
question: Can a slow generator teach a faster one?
intuition: Train a model to replace several small generative steps with a larger jump, an endpoint prediction, or an interval-average velocity.
steps: Identify the trajectory information needed for a large step.
Train a compatible student or self-consistency objective.
Sample using fewer evaluations.
formula: average velocity u = (xₜ − xᵣ)/(t−r), for t ≠ r
example: Instead of asking “which way now?”, ask “what displacement takes me across this whole time interval?”
caveat: These are related motivations, not identical algorithms. MeanFlow can train without a pretrained teacher; consistency models need boundary and consistency conditions.
origin: ATDL topic 2 includes Mean Flows, motivating the distinction between instantaneous and interval-level prediction. The lecture also introduces consistency models.
check: Is average velocity always equal to instantaneous velocity at the interval start?
answer: No. They coincide for a constant-velocity path, but generally differ on curved or changing-speed trajectories.

title: Evaluating generated samples
question: How do we compare generators beyond a few attractive examples?
intuition: Compare quality, diversity and alignment on a sufficiently large, consistently evaluated sample.
steps: Choose features suited to the domain.
Compare real and generated sample distributions.
Report protocol, sample size and complementary checks.
formula: FID compares Gaussian fits to feature means and covariances
example: Two generators may have similar visual sharpness while one repeatedly generates the same few images.
caveat: FID is sample- and feature-dependent; it is not a universal measure of quality. CLIP-based metrics add their own representation biases.
origin: The ATDL generative-model lecture includes FID, Inception Score and CMMD to make evaluation more systematic than inspecting selected images.
check: Why is a hand-picked gallery insufficient evidence of generator quality?
answer: It can hide failures and missing diversity; evaluation needs a representative sampling protocol.

title: Counterfactual explanations
question: What plausible change would make a classifier decide differently?
intuition: Construct a nearby alternative input that changes the prediction while preserving unrelated properties.
steps: Start with a classified example.
Search for a plausible modification toward a target class.
Check that the prediction changes and inspect what else changed.
formula: desired change = prediction flip + plausibility + limited modification
example: An image edit might change a smile while preserving identity; comparing the classifier outputs probes its behavior.
caveat: A model counterfactual is not automatically a real-world causal intervention. A generator may introduce unrelated changes or exploit classifier shortcuts.
origin: DiME uses guided diffusion to produce counterfactual images and evaluates how explanations expose spurious correlations.
check: Why is a tiny adversarial perturbation not necessarily a useful counterfactual explanation?
answer: It may flip the label without representing a human-understandable, plausible change.

title: Representation alignment / REPA
question: Must a generative model discover useful visual features from scratch?
intuition: Use representations from a pretrained visual encoder as an additional learning target for the denoiser’s hidden states.
steps: Encode a clean image with a pretrained visual model.
Project a noisy-input denoiser’s hidden features into a compatible space.
Train with alignment alongside the generative objective.
example: A noisy-image hidden representation learns to agree with semantic features computed from the clean image.
caveat: This transfers a representation preference, not proof that every borrowed feature is useful. Encoder, projection and layer choices matter.
origin: The REPA paper identifies representation learning as a generative-training bottleneck and tests external-feature alignment as a remedy.
check: Does REPA replace the generative training objective?
answer: No. Alignment supplies an additional learning signal alongside generation.

title: Joint image–mask modeling
question: Can segmentation be learned as a relationship inside a joint model?
intuition: Model images and masks together, then use the observed image to guide generation of a compatible pair.
steps: Represent training image–mask pairs jointly.
Learn their shared generative distribution.
At test time guide toward the observed image and recover its corresponding mask.
formula: joint p(image, mask) → infer a compatible mask for an observed image
example: DiffAtlas learns anatomical image–mask relationships rather than only a direct image-to-mask mapping.
caveat: Guided joint sampling is not automatically exact conditional inference. Domain-shift performance is an empirical result, not a guarantee.
origin: DiffAtlas reinterprets atlas-style segmentation using joint image–mask diffusion, studying limited-data and cross-modality settings.
check: What is the central difference from a plain discriminative segmenter?
answer: The joint model learns a distribution over both images and masks, rather than only a direct input-to-mask prediction.

title: In-context image editing
question: How can a generator change an image while remembering what should stay?
intuition: Provide source-image context together with an instruction, so the model can generate a changed view while retaining relevant identity and structure.
steps: Encode source-image context and the edit instruction.
Let the generative model attend to that context.
Generate the target representation and decode the edited image.
formula: context image + instruction + generative state → edited image
example: “Make the jacket blue” should alter jacket color while preserving the person and scene.
caveat: Consistency across repeated edits is measured, not guaranteed. Semantic similarity and precise reconstruction are different demands.
origin: FLUX.1 Kontext uses concatenated context sequences for latent flow-based editing. Qwen-Image distinguishes semantic and reconstructive source-image encodings.
check: Why might a semantic representation alone fail to preserve exact appearance?
answer: It can retain what an object is while discarding fine spatial or visual details needed for reconstruction.

title: MeanFlow: learn the whole jump
question: Can a network predict an interval’s average velocity so generation needs only one jump?
intuition: Replace “how fast right now?” with “what constant velocity would cover the same displacement?” A calculus identity lets us train this interval prediction without computing every true trajectory.
steps: Define average velocity along a trajectory as displacement divided by elapsed time: u(zₜ,r,t)=(zₜ−zᵣ)/(t−r).
Multiply by t−r and differentiate with respect to t, keeping r fixed. The product rule gives u+(t−r)du/dt=v.
Use the chain rule: du/dt=(∂u/∂z)v+∂u/∂t. Compute this directional derivative using a Jacobian-vector product (JVP).
Train uθ against the stopped target (ε−x)−(t−r)JVP(uθ; ε−x). This is a practical network-dependent target, not access to true average velocities.
Generate with zᵣ=zₜ−(t−r)uθ(zₜ,r,t). The full jump uses r=0,t=1.
example: For dz/dt=z with z₁=2, z₀=2/e≈0.73576. Average velocity over [0,1] is 2−2/e≈1.26424; instantaneous velocity at t=1 is 2. Subtracting the average gives the correct endpoint in one step; subtracting the instantaneous velocity gives 0.
caveat: The exact identity concerns the true marginal ODE and assumes sufficient smoothness. Practical training substitutes a neural prediction and sampled conditional velocity. One-step correctness requires an accurate learned interval field; the identity is not a guarantee that optimization recovers it.
origin: Geng et al., Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling (2025), use the relation between average and instantaneous velocity to train a generator without teacher distillation. The discussion here reconstructs the mathematics, not the authors’ private reasoning.
check: Why is an average of the velocities at the two endpoints generally not the MeanFlow target?
answer: The target averages velocity continuously along the trajectory. Two endpoint values give only a trapezoidal approximation, exact under special conditions such as velocity varying linearly with time. MeanFlow learns an interval field, not just the arithmetic mean of two network outputs.

study.subtitle: Keep the path. Change what the network predicts.
study.change: Reuse Flow Matching’s endpoints, noise mixture and backbone. Add a second time and learn average velocity using a derivative correction.

sections.title: Read the symbols before the equations
body: x is a real example; ε (epsilon) is random noise; zₜ is an intermediate state. A state can be one number, a point with two coordinates, or thousands of image-latent coordinates. Bold vectors are not necessary here: the same arithmetic acts on every coordinate.

Throughout these three sections, t=0 means data and t=1 means noise. Generation travels backward, from 1 to 0. This reverses the convention used in some flow-matching presentations but does not change the underlying method. r is an earlier, less noisy time; 0 ≤ r ≤ t ≤ 1. h=t−r is the jump length.

θ (theta) names all learnable network weights. v means instantaneous velocity: motion per unit time right now. u means average velocity over a specified interval. E means an average over random training examples. ‖error‖² means square each coordinate error and add them. sg means keep a computed value but stop gradients through that branch.
sections.formula: zₜ = (1−t)x + tε     h = t−r     v꜀ = ε−x

sections.title: 1. The speedometer and the journey
body: A speedometer gives instantaneous speed. Distance divided by travel time gives average speed. For vector motion we instead divide displacement by time: going out and back can have zero average velocity despite lots of movement. MeanFlow concerns vector displacement, not distance traveled.

Follow the marginal ODE from zₜ backward to zᵣ. The average is the integral of the vector velocity along that same trajectory divided by t−r. It is not an average over training images, nor necessarily the straight conditional pair displacement ε−x.

For the exact toy z(s)=2 exp(s−1), choose t=1 and r=0. The displacement is 1.26424, duration is 1, and the average velocity is 1.26424. The initial instantaneous velocity 2 overestimates the displacement when used for one long backward step.
sections.formula: u(zₜ,r,t) = [1/(t−r)] ∫ᵣᵗ v(zₛ,s) ds = (zₜ−zᵣ)/(t−r)

sections.title: 2. Derive the MeanFlow identity, one operation at a time
body: First multiply by the interval length: (t−r)u=∫ᵣᵗv ds. This removes the fraction and exposes a product.
Now increase the upper time t a little while following the same ODE trajectory and holding r fixed. On the left both the interval length and the average change. The product rule gives u+(t−r)du/dt.
On the right the newly added thin slice contributes v(zₜ,t). This is the fundamental theorem of calculus. Equating the two derivatives and rearranging yields the identity.

The derivative identity plus the regular boundary behavior recovers the displacement definition. If arbitrary singular functions were permitted near t=r, differentiating alone could conceal an integration constant. Smoothness and the limit u(z,t,t)=v(z,t) matter.
sections.formula: (t−r)u = ∫ᵣᵗv ds  →  u+(t−r)du/dt=v  →  u=v−(t−r)du/dt

sections.title: 3. The derivative follows motion, not just the clock
body: The function has three inputs: state z, start time r, end time t. As t changes, z changes along the ODE; r stays fixed. The chain rule adds the effect of moving through space to the effect of the clock changing.

The Jacobian is the table of output changes caused by each input coordinate. We do not need to store that huge table. A JVP asks only how the output changes in one direction: (v,0,1). The 0 means r is fixed and the 1 means t advances at unit speed.

For the scalar network u=a z+b t+c r+d, ∂zu=a and ∂tu=b, so the derivative is a v+b. With a=0.5,b=0.2 and conditional velocity 3, it is 1.7. If h=0.4, the correction is 0.68. With u=0.6, the stopped target is 3−0.68=2.32, error is −1.72, and loss is 2.9584.

Autodiff computes a JVP through the entire network. A finite difference can check a toy derivative, but production JVP is not defined by choosing a tiny finite-difference step. If the implementation uses h=t−r as an input instead of r, its time-direction derivative must account for dh/dt=1.
sections.formula: du/dt = (∂zu)v + ∂tu = JVP(u; (v,0,1))

sections.title: 4. Turning an identity into an algorithm
body: The true marginal velocity and true average field are unknown. The original recipe substitutes the sampled target v꜀=ε−x for the velocity and the current network for the average field inside the derivative. It computes a fresh target from those values.

Stop-gradient keeps the numerical target fixed while calculating a weight update. It does not make the target constant across training: the next update recomputes it with the changed network. This distinction explains why MeanFlow is not ordinary regression on a permanently labeled average velocity.

A batch samples r≤t, with some examples set to r=t so that the correction vanishes and the network also learns the instantaneous boundary. The papers use specific time-sampling distributions and adaptive loss weights; the short code below isolates the core unweighted objective.

At inference, neither JVP nor a training target is required. Draw fresh noise and evaluate uθ(ε,0,1); subtract it from ε. Several shorter interval predictions are also possible. Training costs include derivatives even though sampling may take one model evaluation.
sections.formula: D=JVP(uθ;v꜀); target=sg(v꜀−hD); loss=‖uθ−target‖²; zᵣ=zₜ−h uθ

sections.title: 5. Architecture: a second clock, the same output shape
body: Keep the latent patches, transformer blocks and output projection from the shared image example. The network now needs both where the state is (t) and how far the requested jump reaches (r, or equivalently t−r). These scalar inputs are embedded before conditioning the blocks.

The output is still one vector per latent location. Its interpretation changes from local velocity to interval-average velocity. Nothing requires an output tensor containing all intermediate frames. Inference applies the displacement equation and decodes the endpoint.

Original MeanFlow builds classifier-free guidance into the field during training so guided inference can stay at one evaluation. Its guidance strength is fixed for a trained model in the original formulation; simply mixing conditional and unconditional outputs at sampling would add calls and is not the paper’s one-call recipe.

The JVP is a training calculation around the network, not a special inference layer. The diagram below separates input conditioning, network computation and final sampling. The family of possible backbones remains broader than the particular DiT experiment.
sections.formula: uθ: (zₜ, r, t, class) → average-velocity grid

sections.title: 6. What stays exact, and what can fail?
body: Exact: the definition, product rule and chain rule under regularity assumptions. Approximate: the learned field, sampled conditional replacements and numerical optimization. Empirical: image quality and stability obtained by a particular training recipe.

The identity is compatible with intervals composing: the displacement from t to r equals the displacement from t to s plus that from s to r, where the second prediction must use the transported intermediate state zₛ. Test that state-dependent composition rather than averaging two predictions at the same state.

The next chapter keeps this same sampling rule. It examines a weakness inside training: the compound prediction contains the random pair label through its derivative direction. Rewriting the residual alone will not change the optimization; changing that direction does.
sections.formula: (t−r)u(zₜ,r,t) = (t−s)u(zₜ,s,t) + (s−r)u(zₛ,r,s)

architecture: Same conditional path as Flow Matching
Encode the latent grid as image tokens
Embed t and r (or h=t−r), plus class
uθ(z,r,t) has the shape of z
Training: also compute a directional JVP
Training only; optimize the direct u branch
Inference: no JVP or teacher call
research: Measure interval-composition error at several gaps and boundary error at r=t. Low training loss alone does not establish accurate long jumps.

Hypothesis to test: changing the fraction of boundary examples could improve or harm large-gap learning. Keep total updates fixed, compare several seeds, and report both short- and full-interval errors before making a quality claim.
sources: Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling — Geng et al. (2025), §4 and Algorithms 1–2
Official MeanFlow implementation and training configuration

title: Improved MeanFlow: iMF
question: How can one-step generation keep the MeanFlow idea while improving training and guidance flexibility?
intuition: Keep the average-velocity output and one-jump sampler. Form a velocity prediction whose derivative follows a predicted field, and teach the network to accept guidance settings as explicit inputs.
steps: Reuse the same zₜ, r, t and average-velocity network uθ.
Rearrange the identity into a compound instantaneous prediction Vθ=uθ+(t−r)sg(JVP). Merely moving the derivative term across the loss changes nothing.
Change the JVP direction from ε−x to a prediction vθ, obtained from uθ(z,t,t) or an auxiliary velocity head.
Regress Vθ toward ε−x in the basic unguided objective. The stochastic pair target no longer enters the compound predictor through its tangent.
Condition on guidance scale and interval; use multiple condition tokens alongside latent image tokens. Sample with the same z₀=ε−uθ(ε,0,1,…).
formula: vθ = uθ(zₜ,t,t);    Vθ = uθ(zₜ,r,t)+(t−r)sg[JVP(uθ;vθ)];    LiMF = E[‖Vθ−(ε−x)‖²]
example: Reuse z=0.8,t=0.6,r=0.2 and u=0.5z+0.2t−0.1r+0.1=0.6. The boundary prediction is vθ=0.56. Its JVP is 0.5×0.56+0.2=0.48. Thus V=0.6+0.4×0.48=0.792; against target 3, the squared error is 4.875264. This larger single-example loss does not disprove improved training: the prediction rule has changed.
caveat: Improved Mean Flows (iMF, arXiv:2512.02012) is the paper interpreted here, not the separate paper Understanding, Accelerating, and Improving MeanFlow Training. Better stability and FID are reported empirical results, not universal guarantees. The unguided teaching algorithm omits the full guided target and auxiliary-head recipe.
origin: Geng et al., Improved Mean Flows: On the Challenges of Fastforward Generative Models (2025; CVPR 2026), revisit the original objective, introduce flexible guidance conditioning and change how conditions enter the transformer.
check: Would moving the original stopped JVP term from the target to the prediction, with the same ε−x tangent, already implement iMF?
answer: No. It gives the same residual and the same direct-branch gradient. The core objective change is replacing the sampled conditional tangent with a predicted instantaneous velocity. Flexible guidance and in-context conditioning are further, separate changes.

study.subtitle: Keep the jump. Improve how it is learned and controlled.
study.change: Replace the JVP direction; expose guidance as inputs; replace summed modulation with multiple context tokens. The one-step sampling equation stays the same.

sections.title: Read the symbols before the equations
body: x is a real example; ε (epsilon) is random noise; zₜ is an intermediate state. A state can be one number, a point with two coordinates, or thousands of image-latent coordinates. Bold vectors are not necessary here: the same arithmetic acts on every coordinate.

Throughout these three sections, t=0 means data and t=1 means noise. Generation travels backward, from 1 to 0. This reverses the convention used in some flow-matching presentations but does not change the underlying method. r is an earlier, less noisy time; 0 ≤ r ≤ t ≤ 1. h=t−r is the jump length.

θ (theta) names all learnable network weights. v means instantaneous velocity: motion per unit time right now. u means average velocity over a specified interval. E means an average over random training examples. ‖error‖² means square each coordinate error and add them. sg means keep a computed value but stop gradients through that branch.
sections.formula: zₜ = (1−t)x + tε     h = t−r     v꜀ = ε−x

sections.title: 1. Separate three changes instead of attributing everything to architecture
body: The iMF paper addresses the learning objective, the guidance mechanism and the transformer’s conditioning design. They are related but independently testable choices. A network can use the revised objective without the new conditioning architecture.

The basic derivation below is unguided and uses the boundary prediction rather than an extra head. It makes the central change visible with almost all the preceding chapter’s code reused. The full reported image results include additional recipe choices.
sections.formula: Same path + same interval prediction + same sampler; revised training direction and conditioning

sections.title: 2. First rearrange; then make the actual change
body: Original MeanFlow has residual uθ−sg(v꜀−hD). Since the sampled v꜀ does not depend on θ, it has the same value and direct-branch gradient as uθ+h sg(D)−v꜀. Calling uθ+h sg(D) a compound velocity prediction Vθ does not by itself improve the method.

If D=JVP(uθ;v꜀), this compound prediction uses the pair label v꜀ as an input. Compatible pairs can give different predictions even at the same state and time. A conventional regression predictor instead depends on the known input, not on which hidden endpoint pair supplied the label.

iMF replaces that tangent with a predicted instantaneous velocity. The simplest choice evaluates the same network at zero interval: vθ(z,t)=uθ(z,t,t). Another choice uses a separately trained velocity head sharing the main network. In either case the tangent is predicted from observable state and conditions.

For a scalar affine network, varying the pair tangent by δ changes D by aδ and V by h aδ. Thus conditional tangent variance contributes h²a² Var(v꜀|z,t) to the compound prediction when the coefficients and state are fixed. This algebra explains a possible amplification mechanism; it is not a theorem that all iMF training runs must be more stable.
sections.formula: Original tangent: v꜀=ε−x     →     iMF tangent: vθ(z,t)

sections.title: 3. Why stop-gradient is still here
body: Use the predicted tangent to compute D, then form Vθ=uθ+h sg(D) and regress it toward v꜀. The target of this basic unguided loss is now the usual sampled velocity, with no network-derived term in the label.

The derivative branch remains stopped in the practical algorithm. Gradient descent therefore differentiates the direct uθ prediction while treating D as a constant for that update. This is not the full mathematical gradient of the numerical expression obtained by removing sg.

Without the stop, differentiating the derivative term with respect to weights introduces higher-order differentiation. The paper retains the stop for optimization reasons. Do not implement iMF by merely removing detach from the original MeanFlow target.

At r=t, h=0 and the correction disappears. Both recipes reduce to velocity regression at the boundary. The boundary call may add training work, while the auxiliary-head option changes training capacity; neither adds another generator call to the final one-jump sampler.
sections.formula: D = JVP(uθ; vθ);    Vθ = uθ + h sg(D);    loss = ‖Vθ−v꜀‖²

sections.title: 4. Guidance becomes a requested property of the trajectory
body: Classifier-free guidance combines class-conditional and unconditional instantaneous fields. With the convention below, ω=1 is the conditional field without extra guidance; ω=0 is unconditional, and ω>1 extrapolates toward the class condition. Stronger guidance is not automatically better.

Original MeanFlow learns a field for a fixed guidance setting. iMF gives the network the requested scale ω during training, then allows it to be supplied at inference. It also conditions on the time interval where extra guidance is active, Ω=(ω,tmin,tmax). Outside that interval the guided field uses scale 1.

Even one jump can depend on these interval limits: the predicted average summarizes a trajectory whose instantaneous guidance varies with time. Turning guidance off according only to the starting time of a one-step sampler would not represent that integrated trajectory.

The unguided target ε−x in the miniature algorithm below is not the full CFG training target. The official guided recipe constructs guided targets using network estimates, class-conditioning logic and sampled guidance settings. Adding ω tokens while leaving all targets unguided would teach no meaningful guidance control. Use the linked official implementation for that full recipe.

For the scale-only guided recipe, let ĝc and ĝ∅ be guided boundary velocity predictions with the class present or dropped. The paper’s target is vtarget=(ε−x)+(1−1/ω)(ĝc−ĝ∅), stopped during optimization. The iMF JVP direction is the predicted class-conditioned ĝc. At ω=1 the added target term vanishes. This formula is for positive sampled scales, not ω=0; the cited implementation samples ω≥1. Network-independent targets describe the basic unguided objective, not this self-referential guided extension.

A reconstruction of that target: if the unconditional boundary prediction represents v∅ and the conditional boundary represents g=ωvc+(1−ω)v∅, then g=vc+(1−1/ω)(g−v∅). Replace vc by the sampled ε−x and the unknown fields by current predictions. For a numerical illustration, ω=2, ε−x=3, ĝc=4 and ĝ∅=2 give target 4. This is a bootstrap target calculation, not a ground-truth guided label.
sections.formula: vCFG(z,t|c) = ω v(z,t|c) + (1−ω)v(z,t);    Ω=(ω,tmin,tmax)

sections.title: 5. Architecture: put conditions into the token sequence
body: The latent image path stays familiar: encode → mix → patchify → transformer → unpatchify → velocity grid. The change is how class, time and guidance settings are communicated to the transformer.

Instead of summing condition embeddings for parameter-heavy adaLN-zero modulation, iMF represents each condition using several context tokens and concatenates them with image tokens along the sequence dimension. Attention can read the individual conditions throughout processing. These tokens represent controls, not additional image patches.
